sections.title: Clinical Overview: Advanced Keratoconus
sections.content: Advanced Keratoconus (Stage IV) is characterized by severe corneal thinning (<200μm), extreme steepening (>55D), and the presence of Vogt's striae, Fleischer rings, and potentially apical scarring. When one eye has progressed to surgical intervention (PKP), the fellow eye requires meticulous monitoring and often specialized contact lens fitting or lamellar surgery to maintain visual rehabilitation.

sections.title: The Vascularization Verdict: Deep vs. Superficial

rows: Bypasses the 'immune privilege' by providing direct access for T-lymphocytes and antibodies to the donor stroma and endothelium.
Significant drop; often <50% if >2 quadrants involved

sections.title: Treatment Algorithm: Advanced Keratoconus
content: Step 1: Scleral Lens Trial - Bypasses irregular cornea with a fluid reservoir.
Step 2: CXL (Cross-linking) - Only if cornea >400μm (or use riboflavin-soaked sponge/hypotonic drops).
Step 3: DALK (Deep Anterior Lamellar Keratoplasty) - Preferred if endothelium is healthy; eliminates rejection risk of endothelium.
Step 4: PKP (Penetrating Keratoplasty) - Reserved for full-thickness scars or Descemet's membrane ruptures.

sections.title: Diagnostic Workup for Advanced KC
content: Tomography (Pentacam/Galilei): Posterior elevation is the earliest sign.
AS-OCT: Measure minimum corneal thickness and epithelial mapping.
Specular Microscopy: Assess endothelial health before considering DALK.
Retinoscopy: Scissor reflex is pathognomonic.
Slit Lamp: Fleischer ring (iron at base), Vogt's striae (vertical stress lines).

content.explanation: R: Redness (Perilimbal/Ciliary flush); S: Sensitivity to light (Photophobia); V: Vision decrease (Blurred vision); P: Pain.

sections.title: Red Flags: Acute Hydrops
content: Sudden onset of severe pain
Dramatic drop in vision
White, opaque corneal appearance
Break in Descemet's Membrane
Avoid PKP in acute phase (poor suture hold)

sections.title: Clinical Pearls for Graft Management
content: Suture removal is indicated for vascularization tracking toward the graft-host junction.
Deep vascularization requires aggressive topical steroids (e.g., Pred Forte q1h) and potentially subconjunctival injections.
In the KC eye, scleral lenses can delay the need for surgery by 5-10 years.
Always check for Khodadoust line: a linear precipitate of inflammatory cells on the endothelium.

sections.title: Landmark Study: CLEK
sections.content: The Collaborative Longitudinal Evaluation of Keratoconus (CLEK) study demonstrated that corneal scarring was associated with a higher risk of disease progression and that rigid contact lens wear does not 'stop' the progression of ectasia, though it provides the best visual correction.

sections.title: Recent Advances: CXL Plus
content: Athens Protocol: Simultaneous Topography-guided PRK + CXL.
KeraNatural: Use of gamma-irradiated sterile corneal tissue inlays.
CAIRS: Corneal Allogenic Intrastromal Ring Segments (using donor stroma instead of PMMA).

sections.title: Post-PKP Management Protocol
content: Week 1-4: Pred Forte q2h + Topical Antibiotic qid.
Month 3-6: Suture adjustment/removal based on topography and astigmatism.
Month 12+: Tapering to once-daily steroid (often lifelong in high-risk grafts).
